\chapter{Four Things in a Room --- Door, Window, Chair, Bed}
\label{ch:la-habitacion}
\hlchaptermodality{279}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the door, the window, the chair and the bed in Spanish, and say which of the four has no settled origin.}

Complete ES-C279-cama: name the four things around you, and say which one nobody has managed to trace.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la puerta]{la puerta — a city gate, shrunk to fit a house}

\label{lesson:ES-C279-puerta}



\begin{quote}
Come indoors. The next four words are things in the room you are probably sitting in, and the first of them started life very much larger.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la casa — the house these things are inside.
  \item e $\to$ ie and o $\to$ ue — the two vowels that open under stress.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{PUER-ta}, stress on the first syllable. The \emph{ue} is one glide, not two separate vowels. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la puerta} — \textquotedblleft{}the door.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{porta}, with the short stressed \emph{o} opening into \emph{ue} — the partner of the change that gave you \emph{viento}. Same event, other vowel.

But \emph{porta} did not mean a door in a house. It meant a \textbf{gate}: the opening in a city wall, the thing guarded and shut at night. Spanish took the grand word and let it shrink until it would fit a bedroom.

English holds \emph{porta} in several shapes. A \textbf{portal} is a doorway that still sounds like a gate. A \textbf{porch} came through French from \emph{porticus}, the covered way at the entrance. And one of English's two \textbf{porter}s — the one who keeps the door of a college or a hotel — is the gate-keeper of \emph{porta}, while the porter who carries your luggage comes from a different Latin verb entirely. Two unrelated words, spelled identically, sitting in the same hotel lobby.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Words shrink. A gate in a wall becomes a door in a wall becomes a door in a room, and nothing marks the moment it happened.

This matters for reading older Spanish, where a word you know may still be carrying more weight than it does today. When a text seems to make a small thing sound grand, check whether the word was once grand.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la puerta}, one glide in the middle
  \item what \emph{porta} meant to a Roman (a city gate)
  \item which English \emph{porter} belongs here (the one who keeps the door)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which vowel change turned \emph{porta} into \emph{puerta}? (Stressed \emph{o} opening into \emph{ue}.) What did the Latin word name? (A gate in a city wall.) Which English word keeps that sense most plainly? (\emph{Portal}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la ventana]{la ventana — two languages, one idea, no contact}

\label{lesson:ES-C279-ventana}



\begin{quote}
You met the wind a few lessons ago. It is about to come back indoors, and so is English, by a completely separate road.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el viento — the wind, from Latin \emph{ventus}.
  \item la puerta — the other opening in the wall.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ven-TA-na}, stress in the middle. Three even syllables, no written accent needed because the stress lands where the default puts it. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la ventana} — \textquotedblleft{}the window.\textquotedblright{}

Take Latin \textbf{ventus}, the wind, and add an ending. That is the whole word: a \emph{ventana} is the wind's opening. Notice that the \emph{e} stayed put here — it does not open into \emph{ie}, because in this longer word the stress moved off it and onto the \emph{a}. The change you learned needs a stressed vowel to work on.

Now the good part. English \textbf{window} has nothing to do with Latin. It came from Old Norse \emph{vindauga}, which is \emph{vindr} plus \emph{auga}: \textbf{wind-eye}. Two languages, no contact between them on this point, both looked at a hole in a wall and named it after the draught coming through.

Latin had its own word, \textbf{fenestra}, and Spanish let it go. French and Italian kept it — \emph{fenêtre}, \emph{finestra} — and English borrowed it for one splendid purpose only: \textbf{defenestration}, throwing somebody out of a window.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two things worth carrying out of this one.

First, the sound change has a condition attached. \emph{Ventus} gave \emph{viento} when the \emph{e} was stressed and \emph{ventana} when it was not, and the same vowel behaved differently in the same century for that reason alone.

Second, unrelated languages reach the same metaphor often enough that a shared idea is weak evidence of a shared word. \emph{Ventana} and \emph{window} agree on meaning and share no ancestor at all.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la ventana}, stress in the middle
  \item \emph{el viento}, then \emph{la ventana} — the same Latin word, stressed and unstressed
  \item what \emph{vindauga} meant, part by part (wind, eye)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why does \emph{ventana} keep a plain \emph{e} where \emph{viento} has \emph{ie}? (The stress moved off the vowel.) Which Latin word for a window did Spanish drop? (\emph{Fenestra}.) Where does English still keep it? (\emph{Defenestration}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la silla]{la silla — a word you are sitting on}

\label{lesson:ES-C279-silla}



\begin{quote}
Two openings in the wall, and now the furniture. This word turns out to be a close relative of several English words you would never have guessed.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item sentarse — to sit down, the action this object exists for.
  \item cl-, pl-, fl- $\to$ ll- — the \emph{ll} sound, and where Spanish gets it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{SI-ya} in most of the Spanish-speaking world, \emph{SI-zha} or \emph{SI-sha} around the River Plate. The \emph{ll} is one sound, never two \emph{l} sounds in a row. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la silla} — \textquotedblleft{}the chair.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{sella}, a seat, and behind \emph{sella} the verb \textbf{sedere}, to sit. The object is named after the posture, which is so obvious once said that most people never notice it.

\emph{Sedere} is generous. English \textbf{sedentary} is a life spent sitting. A \textbf{session} is a sitting, which is why parliaments and courts still have them. A \textbf{resident} is somebody sitting back down in a place. The Holy \textbf{See} is a seat, from Latin \emph{sedes}, and a bishop's \textbf{cathedral} is named for his \emph{cathedra}, the chair he speaks from.

And \textbf{saddle} belongs here too, by the cousin route rather than the loan: it comes down the Germanic line from the same ancient root for sitting, without ever passing through Latin.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One root, and you can now recognise it in half a dozen English words you already knew separately.

That is what makes etymology worth the time. You are not memorising trivia about \emph{silla}; you are getting a hook that catches \emph{sedentary}, \emph{session}, \emph{resident} and \emph{cathedral} on the way past — and, next time you meet an unfamiliar Spanish word starting \emph{sed-} or \emph{sen-}, a first guess worth testing.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la silla}, with one \emph{ll} sound
  \item the Latin verb behind it (\emph{sedere}, to sit)
  \item three English words from that verb
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin noun is \emph{silla}? (\emph{Sella}, a seat.) What verb lies behind it? (\emph{Sedere}, to sit.) Is English \emph{saddle} a loan from Latin or a cousin? (A cousin, down the Germanic line.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la cama]{la cama — the second word nobody can explain}

\label{lesson:ES-C279-cama}



\begin{quote}
You have already met one everyday Spanish word with no agreed origin. Here is the other one, and it is even harder to avoid using.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item perro — the dog, and the honest shrug that came with it.
  \item dormir — to sleep.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{CA-ma}, two short even syllables, the \emph{c} hard as in \emph{casa}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la cama} — \textquotedblleft{}the bed.\textquotedblright{}

Latin's word was \textbf{lectum}, and Spanish did keep it: \emph{lecho} survives, but it has gone literary, the sort of bed a character dies in. What you actually sleep in is \emph{cama}, and \emph{cama} is not Latin.

The earliest witness is Isidore of Seville, writing in the 600s, who glosses it as a bed low to the ground and treats it as a local word rather than a Latin one. After that the trail forks. One proposal takes it from Greek \emph{khamai}, \textquotedblleft{}on the ground\textquotedblright{}, which fits Isidore's own definition suspiciously well. Another puts it in the pre-Roman languages of the peninsula, which are barely recorded and so can neither be confirmed nor ruled out.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two of the plainest words in the language — the dog and the bed — have no settled history, and that is not a gap in your notes.

It is worth being clear about why. Both proposals for \emph{cama} predict evidence that would decide the matter, and in both cases the evidence would have had to be written down by people who mostly did not write. The question is open because the record is thin, not because nobody has thought about it.

Meanwhile the word itself is completely secure. You can sleep in a \emph{cama} every night of your life without the etymology ever coming up.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la cama}
  \item the Latin word Spanish half-kept, and what became of it (\emph{lectum}, now the literary \emph{lecho})
  \item the two proposals, and why neither is settled
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \emph{cama} inherited from Latin? (No.) Who is the earliest witness for it? (Isidore of Seville, in the 600s.) Which other everyday word you have already met has the same unsettled status? (\emph{Perro}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
